newsitem.title: USA: Conservative Democrats wary of U.S. budget plan.
newsitem.headline: Conservative Democrats wary of U.S. budget plan.

text.p: A group of conservative House Democrats known as the "Blue Dogs" said Thursday they were wary of reports that a potential balanced budget agreement would not provide for a decline in the deficit each year through 2002.

"While we still don't know the precise path being proposed by the two budget committee chairmen, early information is disturbing," they said at a news conference. "A steady deficit reduction glidepath is critical to any credible budget agreement," they added.

"None of us want a repeat of past deficit redution efforts that have failed to live up to their promises," the Blue Dog coalition said. The budget is a blueprint for federal spending and taxes but does not carry the force of law.

The plan being considered by the White House and congressional leaders would show a rise in the deficit in fiscal 1998 to $90.2 billion. The government's red ink would not fall below 1997's projected $67 billion until fiscal 2001. It shows a small surplus of $1.2 billion in fiscal 2002.

The Blue Dogs have urged that tax cuts be held off until the federal budget is balanced. They also urged the budget accord include an enforcement mechanism to require Congress and the White House to reach a balanced budget.
Enforcement could come through automatic spending cuts or an extension of current caps on annual spending for discretionary programs, they said.
